title: Google Arts & Culture and the Belvedere use machine learning to propose colors for Klimt's destroyed Faculty Paintings, which the Belvedere exhibits in 2025
summary: A colorization model from the Google Arts & Culture Lab proposed colors for photographs of Klimt's destroyed Faculty Paintings, which the Belvedere showed at original size in 2025.
account: Gustav Klimt's Faculty Paintings (Philosophy, Medicine and Jurisprudence) were made for the ceiling of the University of Vienna's Great Hall. Fire destroyed them in 1945; only black-and-white photographs survive. On 7 October 2021 Google Arts & Culture unveiled the online exhibition Klimt vs. Klimt – The Man of Contradictions with the Belvedere. For it, Google Arts & Culture Lab resident Emil Wallner trained a colorization model on 91,749 artworks and then on Klimt's color paintings. Curator Franz Smola's compilation of contemporary descriptions of the colors guided him. On 24 November 2021 Wired published a feature based on its own interviews. In it Smola said that the process re-colorizes the photographs. He said that it does not recreate the original colors. The conservator Ben Fino-Radin called it a misnomer to describe such work as restoration. The Belvedere describes the result as an attempt to reconstruct the original colors in which artificial intelligence played an essential role. It showed the color reconstructions at original size in its exhibition Gustav Klimt – Pigment & Pixel (20 February to 7 September 2025).
purpose: Colorize black-and-white photographs of destroyed paintings in the artist's style, guided by archival color descriptions
system: The Klimt Color Enigma colourisation model (Google Arts & Culture Lab)
deployer: Belvedere, Vienna, with Google Arts & Culture
taxonomy_note: The colorization is a reconstruction hypothesis for destroyed paintings rather than a new creative work.

ratings.reason: The Belvedere adopted the reconstructions and showed them in its 2025 exhibition, according to its exhibition page.
The public can view a hypothesis of the colors of lost works. In a statement that Jing Daily quotes, Smola said that the result was surprising in areas where no knowledge of the colors existed.

ai_role.statement: The model proposed colors for the monochrome photographs. Known colors from Smola's archival research were added directly, so the output mixes documented evidence with learned statistical guesses. The Belvedere calls it an attempt at reconstruction, and no source claims the colors are verified.

comparator.quote: For decades, Klimt's so-called Faculty Paintings, "Philosophy," "Jurisprudence," and "Medicine," have only survived in grainy black-and-white photographs, devoid of the sumptuous, aurous pigment on which the painter's name was made. But no more: on October 7, Google Arts & Culture unveiled Klimt vs. Klimt – The Man of Contradictions, an expansive virtual hub that chronicles Klimt's art and lifetime, and presents a digital reconstruction of his Faculty works — in full and glorious color.

display.answer: The Google Arts & Culture story comes from the makers, and the Belvedere exhibition page comes from the deployer. Jing Daily and I Programmer report the launch and the training of the model. Wired interviewed Smola, Wallner and the independent conservator Ben Fino-Radin.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: A colorization model from the Google Arts & Culture Lab proposed colors for photographs of Klimt's destroyed Faculty Paintings, which the Belvedere showed at original size in 2025.
fields.account: Gustav Klimt's Faculty Paintings (Philosophy, Medicine and Jurisprudence) were made for the ceiling of the University of Vienna's Great Hall. Fire destroyed them in 1945; only black-and-white photographs survive. On 7 October 2021 Google Arts & Culture unveiled the online exhibition Klimt vs. Klimt – The Man of Contradictions with the Belvedere. For it, Google Arts & Culture Lab resident Emil Wallner trained a colorization model on 91,749 artworks and then on Klimt's color paintings. Curator Franz Smola's compilation of contemporary descriptions of the colors guided him. On 24 November 2021 Wired published a feature based on its own interviews. In it Smola said that the process re-colorizes the photographs. He said that it does not recreate the original colors. The conservator Ben Fino-Radin called it a misnomer to describe such work as restoration. The Belvedere describes the result as an attempt to reconstruct the original colors in which artificial intelligence played an essential role. It showed the color reconstructions at original size in its exhibition Gustav Klimt – Pigment & Pixel (20 February to 7 September 2025).
